title: Factotum
full_review:
A factotum is a "man who performs many jobs," as we are duly informed at the start of the credit sequence of this exceedingly bleak adaptation of the late novelist-poet Charles Bukowski's 1975 second novel and some of his other writings.
And indeed, we see Henry "Hank" Chinaski, the heavy-drinking, often brutish, aspiring writer (and Bukowski prototype) drifting from one menial job to another -- delivery man, taxi driver, pickle-factory worker, statue cleaner -- getting fired from each one for bad behavior, in the course of the 93-minute "Factotum" (IFC).

Hank is played by a bearded Matt Dillon, giving a fine performance with laconic, uninflected line readings that seem to perfectly capture Bukowski's melancholy and sardonic musings.

Throughout the film, he falls into relationships with a couple of equally self-destructive losers, fellow boozer Jan (Lili Taylor) and barfly Laura (Marisa Tomei). The sexual encounters are brief, with only fleeting nudity. Through all of this, though, Hank diligently works on his writing, remarkably managing to persevere in submitting his stories for publication, despite continual rejection.

Norwegian writer-director Bent Hamer captures Hank's desolate world with uncompromising exactitude, but the film's pacing is, to put it charitably, deliberate at best. The cinematography is right on the mark in conveying the seamy lowlife ambience. (It was shot in Minneapolis.)

Besides Dillon's fine work, all the actors embody their mostly unlikable characters to a T. While their behavior is reprehensible across the board, the film presents it as such, without glorification.

But the unrelenting ugliness of the story and language, strong sexual elements and overall amoral behavior of its protagonists -- despite the film's literary pedigree -- will seriously limit its appeal.

The film contains pervasive rough and crude language and profanity, rear male and partial female nudity, premarital sexual encounters, gambling, heavy drinking and occasional violence. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
